entries.35aca9c12b285324bc3e0018a9995ec5aae54613: <div sID="gen13015" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="129" osisID="Ps.129" sID="Ps.129"/> <div eID="gen13015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13016" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13017" type="x-p"/> This psalm relates to the public concerns of God's Israel. It is not certain when it was penned, probably when they were in captivity in Babylon, or about the time of their return. I. They look back with thankfulness for the former deliverances God had wrought for them and their fathers out of the many distresses they had been in from time to time, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. They look forward with a believing prayer for and a prospect of the destruction of all the enemies of Zion, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.5-Ps.129.8">ver. 5-8</reference>. In singing this psalm we may apply it both ways to the Gospel-Israel, which, like the Old-Testament Israel, has weathered many a storm and is still threatened by many enemies.
entries.36aa39ca1b09f75bb14638733fe38310f83281cb: <div eID="gen13017" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13016" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Domestic Happiness.</title> <div sID="gen13018" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth, may Israel now say: <hi type="super">2</hi> Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth: yet they have not prevailed against me. <hi type="super">3</hi> The plowers plowed upon my back: they made long their furrows. 4 The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> righteous: he hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked. <div eID="gen13018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13019" type="x-p"/> The church of God, in its several ages, is here spoken of, or, rather, here speaks, as one single person, now old and gray-headed, but calling to remembrance the former days, and reflecting upon the times of old. And, upon the review, it is found, 1. That the church has been often greatly distressed by its enemies on earth: <hi type="italic">Israel may now say,</hi> "I am the people that has been oppressed more than any people, that has been <hi type="italic">as a speckled bird,</hi> pecked at by <hi type="italic">all the birds round about,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Jer.12.9">Jer. xii. 9</reference>. It is true, they brought their troubles upon themselves by their sins; it was for them that God punished them; but it was for the peculiarity of their covenant, and the singularities of their religion, that their neighbours hated and persecuted them. "For these <hi type="italic">many a time have they afflicted me from my youth.</hi>" Note, God's people have always had many enemies, and the state of the church, from its infancy, has frequently been an afflicted state. Israel's youth was in Egypt, or in the times of the Judges; then they were afflicted, and thenceforward more or less. The gospel-church, ever since it had a being, has been at times afflicted; and it bore this yoke most of all in its youth, witness the ten persecutions which the primitive church groaned under. <hi type="italic">The ploughers ploughed upon my back,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">v. 3</reference>. We read (<reference osisRef="Ps.125.3">Ps. cxxv. 3</reference>) of <hi type="italic">the rod of the wicked upon the lot of the righteous,</hi> where we rather expected the plough, to mark it out for themselves; here we read of the <hi type="italic">plough</hi> of the wicked <hi type="italic">upon the back of the righteous,</hi> where we rather expected to find the rod. But the metaphors in these places may be said to be <hi type="italic">crossed;</hi> the sense however of both is the same, and is too plain, that the enemies of God's people have all along used them very barbarously. They tore them, as the husbandman tears the ground with his plough-share, to pull them to pieces and get all they could out of them, and so to <hi type="italic">wear out the saints of the Most High,</hi> as the ground is worn out that has been long tilled, tilled (as we say) quite out of heart. When God permitted them to plough thus he intended it for his people's good, that, their fallow ground being thus broken up, he might sow the seeds of his grace upon them, and reap a harvest of good fruit from them: howbeit, the enemies meant not so, neither did their hearts think so (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">they made long their furrows,</hi> never knew when to have done, aiming at nothing less than the destruction of the church. Many by the <hi type="italic">furrows</hi> they made on the backs of God's people understand the stripes they gave them. <hi type="italic">The cutters cut upon my back,</hi> so they read it. The saints have often <hi type="italic">had trials of cruel scourgings</hi> (probably the captives had) <hi type="italic">and cruel mockings</hi> (for we read of the scourge or lash of the tongue, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.36">Heb. xi. 36</reference>), and so it was fulfilled in Christ, who <hi type="italic">gave his back to the smiters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.6">Isa. l. 6</reference>. Or it may refer to the desolations they made of the cities of Israel. <hi type="italic">Zion shall, for your sake, be ploughed as a field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>. 2. That the church has been always graciously delivered by her friend in heaven. (1.) The enemies' projects have been defeated. They have afflicted the church, in hopes to ruin it, but they have not gained their point. Many a storm it has weathered; many a shock, and many a brunt, it has borne; and yet it is in being: <hi type="italic">They have not prevailed against me.</hi> One would wonder how this ship has lived at sea, when it has been tossed with tempests, and all the waves and billows have gone over it. Christ has built his church upon a rock, and the gates of hell have not prevailed against it, nor ever shall. (2.) The enemies' power has been broken: God <hi type="italic">has cut asunder the cords of the wicked,</hi> has cut their gears, their traces, and so spoiled their ploughing, has cut their scourges, and so spoiled their lashing, has cut the bands of union by which they were combined together, has cut the bands of captivity in which they held God's people. God has many ways of disabling wicked men to do the mischief they design against his church and shaming their counsels. These words, <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous,</hi> may refer either to the distresses or to the deliverances of the church. [1.] <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous</hi> in suffering Israel to be afflicted. This the people of God were always ready to own, that, how unjust soever their enemies were, God was <hi type="italic">just in all that was brought upon them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.9.33">Neh. ix. 33</reference>. [2.] <hi type="italic">The Lord is righteous</hi> in not suffering Israel to be ruined; for he has promised to preserve it a people to himself, and he will be as good as his word. He is righteous in reckoning with their persecutors, and rendering to them <hi type="italic">a recompence,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6">2 Thess. i. 6</reference>.
entries.bc01046ae79ce6b932c43ad34556dc93425d1e84: <div eID="gen13019" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Regard to His Church.</title> <div sID="gen13020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Let them all be confounded and turned back that hate Zion. <hi type="super">6</hi> Let them be as the grass <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the housetops, which withereth afore it groweth up: <hi type="super">7</hi> Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom. <hi type="super">8</hi> Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> upon you: we bless you in the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen13020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13021" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having triumphed in the defeat of the many designs that had been laid as deep as hell to ruin the church, here concludes his psalm as Deborah did her song, <hi type="italic">So let all thy enemies perish, O Lord!</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.5.31">Judg. v. 31</reference>. <div eID="gen13021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13022" type="x-p"/> I. There are many that hate Zion, that hate Zion's God, his worship, and his worshippers, that have an antipathy to religion and religious people, that seek the ruin of both, and do what they can that God may not have a church in the world. <div eID="gen13022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13023" type="x-p"/> II. We ought to pray that all their attempts against the church may be frustrated, that in them they may be <hi type="italic">confounded</hi> and <hi type="italic">turned back</hi> with shame, as those that have not been able to bring to pass their enterprise and expectation: <hi type="italic">Let them all be confounded</hi> is as much as, <hi type="italic">They shall be</hi> all confounded. The confusion imprecated and predicted is illustrated by a similitude; while God's people shall flourish as the loaded palm-tree, or the green and fruitful olive, their enemies shall <hi type="italic">wither as the grass upon the house-top.</hi> As men they are not to be feared, for they shall be made as grass, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa. li. 12</reference>. But as they are enemies to Zion they are so certainly marked for ruin that they may be looked upon with as much contempt as the grass on the house-tops, which is little, and short, and sour, and good for nothing. 1. It perishes quickly: It <hi type="italic">withers before it grows up</hi> to any maturity, having no root; and the higher its place is, which perhaps is its pride, the more it is exposed to the scorching heat of the sun, and consequently the sooner does it wither. <hi type="italic">It withers before it is plucked up,</hi> so some read it. The enemies of God's church wither of themselves, and stay not till they are rooted out by the judgments of God. 2. It is of no use to any body; nor are <hi type="italic">they</hi> any thing but the unprofitable burdens of the earth, nor will their attempts against Zion ever ripen or come to any head, nor, whatever they promise themselves, will they get any more by them than the husbandman does by the grass on his house-top. Their <hi type="italic">harvest will be a heap in the day of grief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.17.11">Isa. xvii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen13023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13024" type="x-p"/> III. No wise man will pray God to bless the mowers or reapers, <reference osisRef="Ps.129.8">v. 8</reference>. Observe, 1. It has been an ancient and laudable custom not only to salute and wish a good day to strangers and travellers, but particularly to pray for the prosperity of harvest-labourers. Thus Boas prayed for his reapers. <reference osisRef="Ruth.2.4">Ruth ii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">The Lord be with you.</hi> We must thus acknowledge God's providence, testify our good-will to our neighbours, and commend their industry, and it will be accepted of God as a pious ejaculation if it come from a devout and upright heart. 2. Religious expressions, being sacred things, must never be made use of in light and ludicrous actions. Mowing the grass on the house-top would be a jest, and therefore those that have a reverence for the name of God will not prostitute to it the usual forms of salutation, which savoured of devotion; for holy things must not be jested with. 3. It is a dangerous thing to let the church's enemies have our good wishes in their designs against the church. If we <hi type="italic">wish them God speed, we are partakers of their evil deeds,</hi> <reference osisRef="2John.1.11">2 John 11</reference>. When it is said, None will bless them, and show them respect, more is implied, namely, that all wise and good people will cry out shame on them, and beg of God to defeat them; and woe to those that have the prayers of the saints against them. <hi type="italic">I cursed his habitation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.5.3">Job v. 3</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.129"/> <div eID="gen13024" type="x-p"/>

entries.2ffbcc04ddb7a8a4414455d3bc521ced2aea3f0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7027"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 129</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:1-8</reference>. The people of God, often delivered from enemies, are confident of His favor, by their overthrow in the future.</title> <div sID="gen10782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7027"/><hi type="bold">1-2. may Israel now say--</hi>or, "oh! let Israel say" (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.1">Psa 124:1</reference>). Israel's youth was the sojourn in Egypt (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jr 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Ho 2:15</reference>). <div eID="gen10782" type="x-p"/>
entries.d180db319e17a62e159449a13daa8832920a9628: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7029"/><div sID="gen10784" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7029"/>3-4. The ploughing is a figure of scourging, which most severe physical infliction aptly represents all kinds. <div eID="gen10784" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b3ac9b6709ccf2da29511d325c580daf9378390: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7031"/><div sID="gen10786" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7031"/>5-6. The ill-rooted roof grass, which withers before it grows up and procures for those gathering it no harvest blessing (<reference osisRef="Ruth.2.4">Ru 2:4</reference>), sets forth the utter uselessness and the rejection of the wicked. <chapter eID="Ps.129"/>

entries.22b922cd96023a87a05b2fb8c0c6408fdc4279a9: <div eID="gen23133" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23134" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23135" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23135" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23134" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23136" type="x-p"/> The Jews give an account of the afflicions which they have passed through, <reference osisRef="Psa.129.1-Psa.129.3">Psa 129:1-3</reference>. And thank God for their deliverance, <reference osisRef="Psa.129.4">Psa 129:4</reference>. The judgments that shall fall on the workers of iniquity, <reference osisRef="Psa.129.5-Psa.129.8">Psa 129:5-8</reference>. <div eID="gen23136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23137" type="x-p"/> This Psalm was written after the captivity; and contains a reference to the many tribulations which the Jews passed through from their youth, i.e., the earliest part of their history, their bondage in Egypt. It has no title in any of the Versions, nor in the Hebrew text, except the general one of A Psalm of Degrees. The author is uncertain. <div eID="gen23137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23138" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23139" type="x-p"/> Many a time have they afflicted me - The Israelites had been generally in affliction or captivity from the earliest part of their history, here called their youth. So <reference osisRef="Hos.2.15">Hos 2:15</reference> : "She shall sing as in the days of her youth, when she came up out of the land of Egypt." See <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Eze.16.4">Eze 16:4</reference>, etc.
entries.0351c402cd1d2b19631e91ead3ba76b989cffb8e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23140" type="x-p"/> Yet they have not prevailed - They endeavored to annihilate us as a people; but God still preserves us as his own nation.
entries.f8ea8dbb4da70b7cd2ed8f63ee1a3e11af38ce91: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23141" type="x-p"/> The plowers plowed upon my back - It is possible that this mode of expression may signify that the people, during their captivity, were cruelly used by scourging, etc.; or it may be a sort of proverbial mode of expression for the most cruel usage. There really appears here to be a reference to a yoke, as if they had actually been yoked to the plouph, or to some kind of carriages, and been obliged to draw like beasts of burden. In this way St. Jerome understood the passage; and this has the more likelihood, as in the next verse God is represented as cutting them off from these draughts.
entries.d6b82baba0b42190a2eb8f205e0cdf8ce0dbc36e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23142" type="x-p"/> The Lord - hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked - The words have been applied to the sufferings of Christ; but I know not on what authority. No such scourging could take place in his case, as would justify the expression: - "The ploughers made long furrows there, <div eID="gen23142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23143" type="x-p"/> Till all his body was one wound." <div eID="gen23143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23144" type="x-p"/> It is not likely that he received more than thirty-nine stripes. The last line is an unwarranted assertion.
entries.b68a6af9d7a91fdd4b0130ff312d8ef8516302bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23145" type="x-p"/> Let them all be confounded - They shall be confounded. They who hate Zion, the Church of God, hate God himself; and all such must be dealt with as enemies, and be utterly confounded.
entries.35c4797279d1247d9267074b81af9d95e4b36de2: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23146" type="x-p"/> As the grass upon the housetops - As in the east the roofs of the houses were flat, seeds of various kinds falling upon them would naturally vegetate, though in an imperfect way; and, because of the want of proper nourishment, would necessarily dry and wither away. If grass, the mower cannot make hay of it; if corn, the reaper cannot make a sheaf of it. Let the Babylonians be like such herbage - good for nothing, and come to nothing. <div eID="gen23146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23147" type="x-p"/> Withereth afore it groweth up - Before שלק shalak, it is unsheathed; i.e., before it ears, or comes to seed.
entries.2aa5523fd5f5cbc4293afe03d94d88ca7f063251: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23148" type="x-p"/> Neither do they which go by say - There is a reference here to the salutations which were given and returned by the reapers in the time of the harvest. We find that it was customary, when the master came to them into the field, to say unto the reapers, The Lord be with you! and for them to answer, The Lord bless thee! <reference osisRef="Rut.2.4">Rut 2:4</reference>. Let their land become desolate, so that no harvest shall ever more appear in it. No interchange of benedictions between owners and reapers. This has literally taken place: Babylon is utterly destroyed; no harvests grow near the place where it stood.  <chapter eID="Ps.129"/> <div eID="gen23148" type="x-p"/>

entries.fd0040a04aa7ae71b50f8d65559388e8ab7d5d5c: The End of the Oppressors of Zion <div eID="gen10207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10208" type="x-p"/> Just as <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8">Psa 124:1-8</reference> with the words <hi type="italic">“let Israel say”</hi> was followed by <reference osisRef="Ps.125.1-Ps.125.5">Psa 125:1-5</reference> with <hi type="italic">“peace be upon Israel,”</hi> so <reference osisRef="Ps.128.1-Ps.128.6">Psa 128:1-6</reference> with <hi type="italic">“peace be upon Israel”</hi> is followed by <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:1-8</reference> with <hi type="italic">“let Israel say.”</hi> This <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:1-8</reference> has not only the call <hi type="italic">“let Israel say,”</hi> but also the situation of a deliverance that has been experienced (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.129.4">Psa 129:4</reference> with Psa 124:6.), from which point it looks gratefully back and confidently forward into the future, and an Aramaic tinge that is noticeable here and there by the side of all other classical character of form, in common with <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1">Psa 124:1</reference>-8.
entries.f9e97037ccc6168041f057c618befdf903d31b80: <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.2">Psa 129:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen10208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10209" type="x-p"/> Israel is gratefully to confess that, however much and sorely it was oppressed, it still has not succumbed. רבּת, together with רבּה, has occurred already in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.10">Psa 65:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Psa 62:3</reference>, and it becomes usual in the post-exilic language, <reference osisRef="Ps.120.6">Psa 120:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Psa 123:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.18">2Ch 30:18</reference>; Syriac <hi type="italic">rebath</hi>. The expression “from my youth” glances back to the time of the Egyptian bondage; for the time of the sojourn in Egypt was the time of Israel’s youth (Hos 2:17, Hos 11:1, <reference osisRef="Jer.2.2">Jer 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.3">Eze 23:3</reference>). The protasis <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.129.1">Psa 129:1</reference></hi> is repeated in an interlinked, chain-like conjunction in order to complete the thought; for <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.129.2">Psa 129:2</reference></hi> is the turning-point, where גּם, having reference to the whole negative clause, signifies “also” in the sense of “nevertheless,” ὅμως (synon. בּכל־בּכל), as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.28">Eze 16:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ecc 6:7</reference>, cf. above, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.24">Psa 119:24</reference> : although they oppressed me much and sore, yet have they not overpowered me (the construction is like Num 13:30, and frequently).
entries.a2e3c3db93b22bdf94fa4b1969b8c908f89dc7c7: <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3-Ps.129.5">Psa 129:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen10209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10210" type="x-p"/> Elsewhere it is said that the enemies have driven over Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.12">Psa 66:12</reference>), or have gone over its back (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Isa 51:23</reference>); here the customary figurative language חרשׁ און in <reference osisRef="Job.4.8">Job 4:8</reference> (cf. Hos 10:13) is extended to another figure of hostile dealing: without compassion and without consideration they ill-treated the stretched-forth back of the people who were held in subjection, as though it were arable land, and, without restraining their ferocity and setting a limit to their spoiling of the enslaved people and country, they drew their furrow-strip (מעניתם, according to the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> מענותם) long. But מענה does not signify (as Keil on <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.14">1Sa 14:14</reference> is of opinion, although explaining the passage more correctly than Thenius) the furrow (= תּלם, גּדוּד), but, like Arab. <hi type="italic">ma‛nât</hi>, a strip of arable land which the ploughman takes in hand at one time, at both ends of which consequently the ploughing team (צמד) always comes to a stand, turns round, and ploughs a new furrow; from ענה, to bend, turn (vid., Wetzstein’s Excursus II p. 861). It is therefore: they drew their furrow-turning long (dative of the object instead of the accusative with <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.2">Isa 29:2</reference>, cf. with <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.34.4">Psa 34:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>, and <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.69.6">Psa 69:6</reference>, after the Aramaic style, although it is not unhebraic). Righteous is Jahve - this is an universal truth, which has been verified in the present circumstances; - He hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked (עבות as in <reference osisRef="Ps.2.3">Psa 2:3</reference>; here, however, it is suggested by the metaphor in <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.39.10">Job 39:10</reference>; lxx αὐχένας, i.e., ענוק), with which they held Israel bound. From that which has just been experienced Israel derives the hope that <hi type="italic">all</hi> Zion’s haters (a newly coined name for the enemies of the religion of Israel) will be obliged to retreat with shame and confusion.
entries.2a46674aac0027b670b904fd2398b9b40fa13604: <reference osisRef="Ps.129.6-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen10210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10211" type="x-p"/> The poet illustrates the fate that overtakes them by means of a picture borrowed from Isaiah and worked up (<reference osisRef="Ps.37.27">Psa 37:27</reference>): they become like “grass of the housetops,” etc. שׁ is a relative to יבשׁ (<hi type="italic">quod exarescit</hi>), and קדמת, <hi type="italic">priusquam</hi>, is Hebraized after מן־קדמת דּנה in <reference osisRef="Dan.6.11">Dan 6:11</reference>, or מקּדמת דּנה in Ezr 5:11. שׁלף elsewhere has the signification “to draw forth” of a sword, shoe, or arrow, which is followed by the lxx, Theodotion, and the Quinta: πρὸ τοῦ ἐκσπασθῆναι, before it is plucked. But side by side with the ἐκσπασθῆναι of the lxx we also find the reading exanthee'sai; and in this sense Jerome renders (<hi type="italic">statim ut</hi>) <hi type="italic">viruerit</hi>, Symmachus ἐκκαυλῆσαι (to shoot into a stalk), Aquila ἀνέθαλεν, the Sexta ἐκστερεῶσαι (to attain to full solidity). The Targum paraphrases שׁלף in both senses: to shoot up and to pluck off. The former signification, after which Venema interprets: <hi type="italic">antequam se evaginet vel evaginetur,</hi> i.e., <hi type="italic">antequam e vaginulis suis se evolvat et succrescat</hi>, is also advocated by Parchon, Kimchi, and Aben-Ezra. In the same sense von Ortenberg conjectures שׁחלף. Since the grass of the house-tops or roofs, if one wishes to pull it up, can be pulled up just as well when it is withered as when it is green, and since it is the most natural thing to take חציר as the subject to שׁלף, we decide in favour of the intransitive signification, “to put itself forth, to develope, shoot forth into ear.” The roof-grass withers before it has put forth ears of blossoms, just because it has no deep root, and therefore cannot stand against the heat of the sun.<note placement="foot">So, too, Geiger in the <hi type="italic">Deutsche Morgenländische Zeitschrift</hi>, xiv. 278f., according to whom Arab. <hi type="italic">slf</hi> (<hi type="italic">šlf</hi>) occurs in Saadia and Abu-Said in the signification “to be in the first maturity, to blossom,” - a sense שׁלף may also have here; cf. the Talmudic שׁלופפי used of unripe dates that are still in blossom.</note> <div eID="gen10211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10212" type="x-p"/> The poet pursues the figure of the grass of the house-tops still further. The encompassing lap or bosom (κόλπος) is called elsewhere חצן (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.22">Isa 49:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.13">Neh 5:13</reference>); here it is חצן, like the Arabic <hi type="italic">ḥiḍn</hi> (diminutive <hi type="italic">ḥoḍein</hi>), of the same root with מחוז, a creek, in Psa 107:30. The enemies of Israel are as grass upon the house-tops, which is not garnered in; their life closes with sure destruction, the germ of which they (without any need for any rooting out) carry within themselves. The observation of Knapp, that any Western poet would have left off with <reference osisRef="Ps.129.6">Psa 129:6</reference>, is based upon the error that <reference osisRef="Ps.129.7-Ps.129.8">Psa 129:7-8</reference> are an idle embellishment. The greeting addressed to the reapers in <reference osisRef="Ps.129.8">Psa 129:8</reference> is taken from life; it is not denied even to heathen reapers. Similarly Boaz (Rth 2:4) greets them with “Jahve be with you,” and receivers the counter-salutation, “Jahve bless thee.” Here it is the passers-by who call out to those who are harvesting: <hi type="italic">The blessing</hi> (בּרכּת) <hi type="italic">of Jahve</hi> <hi type="italic">happen to you</hi> (אליכם,<note placement="foot">Here and there עליכם is found as an error of the copyist. The <hi type="italic">Hebrew</hi> <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, Basel 1547, 12mo, notes it as a various reading.</note> as in the Aaronitish blessing), and (since “we bless you in the name of Jahve” would be a purposeless excess of politeness in the mouth of the same speakers) receive in their turn the counter-salutation: <hi type="italic">We bless you in the name of Jahve</hi>. As a contrast it follows that there is before the righteous a garnering in of that which they have sown amidst the exchange of joyful benedictory greetings.  <chapter eID="Ps.129"/> <div eID="gen10212" type="x-p"/>

entries.5c83bfa9a96e47ef9ea6d966b00c6bdde44c8ec2:
PSALM 129
This Psalm teaches, in the first place, that God subjects his Church to divers troubles and affections, to the end he may the better prove himself her deliverer and defender. The Psalmist, therefore, recalls to the memory of the faithful how sadly God’s people had been persecuted in all ages, and how wonderfully they had been preserved, in order by such examples to fortify their hope in reference to the future. In the second part, under the form of an imprecation, he shows that the divine vengeance is ready to fall upon all the ungodly, who without cause distress the people of God.
A Song of Degrees.
Psalm 129:1-4
1. They have often afflicted me from my youth, let Israel now say: 2. They have often afflicted me from my youth; but they have not prevailed against me. 3. The ploughers have plouched upon my back, and made long their furrows.
“Targ. lengthened out their ploughing, i.e., gave us no rest from their slavery, for the longer the furrows the more tedious is the labor of the oxen.” — Bythner.
4. But Jellovah who is righteous, hath cut asunder the cords of the wicked.
 
1. They have often afflicted me from my youth. This Psalm was probably composed at a time when the Church of God, reduced to a state of extreme distress, or dismayed by some great danger, or oppressed with tyranny, was on the verge of total destruction. This conjecture, I conceive, is supported by the adverb of time, now, which appears to me to be emphatic. It is as if the Prophet; had said, When God’s faithful ones are with difficulty drawing their breath under the burden of temptations, it is a seasonable time for them to reflect on the manner in which he has exercised his people from the beginning, and from age to age. As soon as God has given loose reins to our enemies to do as they please we are distressed with sorrow, and our thoughts are wholly engrossed with the evils which presently harass us. Hence proceeds despair; for we do not remember that the patience of the fathers was subjected to the like trial, and that nothing happens to us which they did not experience. It is then an exercise eminently fitted to comfort true believers to look back to the conflicts of the Church in the days of old, in order thereby to know that she has always labored under the cross, and has been severely afflicted by the unrighteous violence of her enemies. The most probable conjecture which occurs to me at present is, that this Psalm was written after the Jews had returned from the Babylonish captivity, and when, having suffered many grievous and cruel injuries at the hands of their neighbors, they hadn’t length almost fainted under the tyranny of Antiochus Epiphanes. In this dark and troublous state of matters, the Prophet encourages the faithful to fortitude, nor does he address himself to a few of them only, but to the whole body without exception; and in order to their sustaining such fierce assaults, he would have them to oppose to them a hope inspired by the encouraging consideration, that the Church, by patient endurance, has uniformly proved victorious. Almost every word is emphatic. Let Israel now say, that is, let him consider the trials of the Church in ancient times, from which it may be gathered, that the people of God have never been exempted from bearing the cross, and yet that the various afflictions by which they have been tried have always had a happy issue. In speaking of the enemies of Israel simply by the pronoun they, without being more specific, the Psalmist aggravates the greatness of the evil more than if he had expressly named the Assyrians or the Egyptians. By not specifying any particular class of foes, he tacitly intimates that the world is fraught with innumerable bands of enemies, whom Satan easily arms for the destruction of good men, his object being that new wars may arise continually on every side. History certainly bears ample testimony that the people of God had not to deal with a few enemies, but that they were assaulted by almost the whole world; and farther, that they were molested not only by external foes, but also by those of an internal kind, by such as professed to belong to the Church.
The term youth here denotes their first beginnings,
Hence it is said in Hosea 11:1 —
“When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.”
Youth is in like manner ascribed to a people, in Isaiah 47:12, 15; Jeremiah 48:11; and Ezekiel 16:43.
and refers not only to the time when God brought the people out of Egypt, but also to the time when he wearied Abraham and the patriarchs during almost their whole life, by keeping them in a condition of painful warfare. If these patriarchs were strangely driven about in the land of Canaan, the lot of their descendants was still worse during the time of their sojourning in Egypt, when they were not only oppressed as slaves, but loaded with every kind of reproach and ignominy. At their departure from that land we know what difficulties they had to encounter. If in tracing their history from that period we find seasons in which some respite was granted them, yet they were not in a state of repose for any length of time, until the reign of David. And although during his reign they appeared to be in a prosperous condition, yet soon after troubles and even. defeats arose, which threatened the people of God with total destruction. In the Babylonish captivity, all hope being well-nigh extinguished, they seemed as if hidden in the grave and undergoing the process of putrefaction. After their return they obtained, with difficulty, some brief intermission to take their breath. They were certainly often put; to the sword, until the race of them was almost wholly destroyed. To prevent it, therefore, from being supposed that they had received only some slight hurt, they are justly said to have been afflicted; as if the Prophet placed them before our eyes as it were half-dead, through the treatment of their enemies, who, seeing them prostrated under their feet, scrupled not to tread upon them. If we come to ourselves, it will be proper to add the horrible persecutions, by which the Church would have been consumed a thousand times, had not God, by hidden and mysterious means, preserved her, raising her as it were from the dead. Unless we have become stupid under our calamities, the distressing circumstances of this unhappy age will compel us to meditate on the same doctrine.
When the Prophet says twice, they have afflicted me, they have afflicted me, the repetition is not superfluous, it being intended to teach us that the people of God had not merely once or twice to enter the conflict, but that their patience had been tried by continual exercises. He had said that they had commenced this conflict from their youth, intimating that they had been inured to it from their first origin, in order to their being accustomed to bear the cross. He now adds, that their being subjected to this rigorous training was not without good reason, inasmuch as God had not ceased, by a continued course, to make use of these calamities for subduing them to himself. If the exercises of the Church, during her state of childhood, were so severe, our effeminacy will be very shameful indeed, if in the present day, when the Church, by the coming of Christ, has reached the age of manhood, we are found wanting in firmness for enduring trials. Matter of consolation is laid down in the last clause, which informs us that the enemies of Israel, after having tried all methods, never succeeded in realizing their wishes, God having always disappointed their hopes, and baffled their attempts.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="129" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXIX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains a joyful and thankful remembrance of the Churches former and manifold calamities from barbarous enemies, and of Gods wonderful mercy in delivering them out of their hands.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> much.</ns0:note> MAny a time have they <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Mine enemies or oppressors; which is easily understood both from the nature of the thing, and from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 3. where they are expressed under the name of <ns0:hi>plowers.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> afflicted me from my youth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">From the time that I was a people, when I was in <ns0:hi>Egypt</ns0:hi> and came out of it, which is called the time of <ns0:hi>Israels youth, Ier.</ns0:hi> 2. 2. <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 23. 3.</ns0:note>, may <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 124. 1.</ns0:note> Israel now say.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth: yet they have not prevailed against me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 The plowers plowed upon my back <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">They have not onely thrown me down and trod me un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der foot, but have cruelly tormented me, wounded and mangled me, and had no more pity upon me than the plow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man hath upon the earth which he cuts up at his pleasure. He saith, <ns0:hi>upon my back,</ns0:hi> either because they did literally scourge the Captives upon their backs with such <ns0:hi>cords</ns0:hi> as are mentioned <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 4. although we do not read that the Israelitish Captives were thus used by any of their enemies; or by way of allusion to that usage, which made a sort of furrows in their backs upon which they used to lay on their strokes.</ns0:note>: they made long their furrows <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">They oft repeated their injuries and prolonged my tor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 The LORD <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> righteous <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Faithful or merciful, as that word is frequently used.</ns0:note>: he hath cut a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sunder the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 140. 5.</ns0:note> cords <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Wherewith the plow was drawn; by which means they were stopped in their course. So he persists in the same Me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />taphor of a plough. By these <ns0:hi>cords</ns0:hi> he understands all their plots and endeavours.</ns0:note> of the wicked.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Let them all be confounded and turned back <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Forced to retreat with shame and disappointment.</ns0:note> that hate Zion.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Let them be as the grass <ns0:hi>upon</ns0:hi> the house<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tops <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Which there were flat, and therefore more capable of grass, or green corn growing between the stones, than ours are.</ns0:note>, which withereth afore it groweth up <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which having no deep root, never comes to matu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity. And so all their designs shall be abortive and never come to perfection.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand; nor he that bindeth sheaves, his bosom.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Neither do they which go by say, The bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sing of the LORD <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> upon you <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which was an usual salutation given by passengers to reapers, as <ns0:hi>Ruth</ns0:hi> 2. 4. So the meaning is, It never continues till the harvest comes.</ns0:note>: we bless you in the name of the LORD.</ns0:p>
